7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is B. Qa7. From a2, shifting to a7 keeps the queen active on the a-file while eyeing the e3 rook indirectly and preventing white's king from easily escaping to the g-file or supporting the e-pawn advance without allowing perpetual checks or a trade that leads to a drawn rook ending. It also maintains pressure on the f2/g2 area in some lines, which seems more forcing than retreating to the back rank or shifting to the d-file.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think B. Qa7 is the key drawing resource here. After 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3, Qa7 keeps the queen active on the a-file and eyes potential checks along the seventh rank once the rook moves. It also maintains some distance from the white knight on h5, avoiding immediate forks while still threatening to swing over for perpetual checks against the exposed king on h3. The e6-pawn is advanced but the black king can likely step to f8 or g8 in time to contain it, and white's rook on f7 isn't ideally placed to coordinate a mating net without allowing the queen to deliver repeated checks from a7-b8 or similar squares. This seems like the most practical way to hold the half-point rather than allowing white to consolidate with the advanced pawns.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: N. Qa3
After 130.Kh3 the key is to keep giving checks while avoiding the fork on f7 or the advance of the f-pawn. Qa3+ forces the king to either h4 (where …Qe7+ or …Qf3+ ideas become available) or g4 (where …Qe2+ picks up the knight or forces a repetition). In both cases Black keeps the king exposed and can cycle checks between the a-file and the second rank, which should be enough to hold the draw. The other listed squares either allow White to consolidate with Ng7 or lose the queen to a knight fork.

1.text:
After 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king is on h3, Ng3, Rf5, e5 f4 h4
and the black king is on e8.  The only squares from which the queen
can actually give a real check on h3 are g2 and h2.  Qg2+ is met by
Kxg2 and Qh2+ is met by ...Kg4 or Kxh2, so the two checks are not
usable.

What black needs is a waiting move which keeps the queen in
perpetual-checking distance of h3 and which does not allow White to
make any useful progress with the Rf5–Ng3 battery.  That is obtained
by keeping the queen on the 2nd rank, or on the a-file just in front
of the Ng3–blocker, so that the queen can shuttle back and forth
between the 2nd rank and, when the knight has to move, to g3.

In particular the whole family

130...Qb2  130...Qc2  130...Qd2  130...Qe2  130...Qf2

is a waiting move. The queen stays on the 2nd rank and can at any
time go Qg2+ or Qh2+ and the king has only g4 and the capturing
squares g2/h2 at its disposal, i.e. a forced perpetual.  The same
idea is the a-file waiting move

130...Qa1     130...Qa3

which attacks the Ng3 blocker and threatens the perpetual
Qxg3+–Qa1–Qa3...  Qa3 is the move that is usually quoted, 

130...Qa3  131.Rf3 Qa1  132.Rg3 Qb2  133... 

and after any White king or rook move Black has Qh2+ / Qg2+ or
Qxg3+ with an immediate draw by repetition.  Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qe2 and
Qf2 are the same idea on the second rank.  Qa1 and Qa3 are the
text-book waiting moves; Qg2+ and Qh2+ are immediate checks which
lose the queen and Qe6 is the losing blunder played in the game.

3.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white pawn on e4 has just been
advanced to e5

```
1. … R f5-e5
```

The capture Rxe5 is now a forced winning threat.  After Rxe5 the rook
stands on e5 and controls the whole 5th rank and the whole e-file.
In particular

* every queen on the 5th rank a5-b5-c5-d5-f5-g5-h5 and
* every queen on the e-file e2-e3-e4-e6-e7-e8

is immediately lost to the rook after the capture.

The queen is on a2.  The only way to keep the queen out of the
rook’s 5th rank/e-file net and at the same time to keep the
perpetual-checking resource on the h–file is to retreat the queen
on the a-file.  From the a-file the queen can always be taken to the
h-file on the same rank, e.g.

    Qa1 – Qh1+ , Qa4 – Qh4+ , Qa6 – Qh6+ , etc.

and the checks can be repeated until the white king is destroyed.
The position is then a normal queen-vs-rook+knight draw.  The
text-book illustration of the resource is the retreat to the first
rank

130… Qa1

and in fact Qa3, Qa4, Qa6, Qa7 and Qa8 are the same kind of
a-file retreats.  The move actually played,

130… Qe6,

puts the queen on the e-file.  After 131 Rxe5 the queen is on the
same file as the rook on e5, e.g. 131… Qe6 Rxe5 Qxe5+ etc., and the
black queen is lost.  The 5th-rank move 130… Qa5 and the e-file move
130… Qe2 suffer from the same Rxe5 refutation.  This is the
well-known loss of the 136-move Game 6 draw.

2.text:
In the position after 29.e5 Qa2+ 30.Kh3 the white king is on h3,
the white knight is on g3 and the white e-pawn is on e5.  The only way
for White to make progress is e6 with the threat of e7–e8.  On a2 the
queen covers e6, a2–b3–c4–d5–e6, and after 30...Qe6 the square e6 is
uncovered and 31.Kh4 Qh6+ 32.Nh5 etc. is the winning continuation which
was actually played.

If the queen stays on the a-file it can be kept on the same
a1–e5 / a2–e6 diagonal and at the same time it can be brought round
to the h-file for a perpetual.  In particular

30… Qa1

keeps the queen on the a-file, 31…Qh1+ 32.Kg4 Qh2+ 33.Kf5 Qe5+ and so
on, and White can never give up the e-pawn because the queen is always
able to interpose on e5/e6.  The same idea is obtained with any
a-file retreat,

Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8,

and, up to the rook on e2, with the 2nd–rank retreats Qb2, Qc2, Qd2,
Qe2, which allow …Qh2+ on the next move.  The move most often quoted
is the text-book 130… Qa1 – 130… Qa3 is the same idea in one move –
and it is the perpetual which Nepo missed with the losing 130…Qe6.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The queen has to stay on the a – file.  After 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the
white king is on h3, the white rook is on f5 and the e-pawn is on e5.  
In particular the e-pawn can be stopped at once on the same rank as the
queen.  The a-file retreat keeps the queen out of the rook–knight net and
keeps the e-pawn under control, the ordinary perpetual that is quoted
in the literature being

130… Qa1 !

With the queen on the a-file the e-pawn can never be let through to
e6/e7/e8 and Black can go on giving checks on the 2nd/3rd rank.  The
same idea is obtained with any a-file retreat – Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6,
Qa7, Qa8 – the most forcing of them being the 6th rank block
130… Qa6 which meets e6 with Qxe6.  Qa1 is the move that is normally
quoted for the draw.

3.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the black queen is on a2 and the only thing
which White can do with the material is to try the e–pawn.  From a2 the
queen covers e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal and, on the same rank, she can
come to h2/g2 with an immediate check on the h–file

    a2–h2+ , a2–g2+

so that the king on h3 can be forced into an eternal check.  The
perpetual is kept alive as long as the queen stays on the 2nd rank or,
what is the same thing, on the a–file where she can be brought back to
the 2nd rank at will.  In particular the whole second rank family

130…Qb2 , 130…Qc2 , 130…Qd2 , 130…Qe2 , 130…Qf2

is a waiting move and after any 131 e6 White is met by …Qxe6 in the
a2–e6 diagonal sense or, more simply, by a perpetual …Qh2+/…Qg2+.
The same waiting idea is obtained on the a–file.  The text-book
illustration is

130…Qa1!

and, up to symmetry, any a–file retreat which keeps the e-pawn under
control.  The move most often quoted in the literature is the one
move waiting move

130…Qa3!

After 130…Qa3! 131 e6 is met by the perpetual 131…Qxg3+ 132 Kxg3
Qh3+ etc., 131 Rf6 is met by 131…Qh3+ 132 Kg4 Qh4+ and so on, and the
White king can never escape the rook–knight battery without allowing a
repeat of …Qh2+/…Qg2+.  Qa1 is the same idea on the first rank and
Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2 are the same second-rank waiting moves.  Qa4 is the
same a-file idea, the first a-file square which still keeps h4 in play.
The blunder 130…Qe6 puts the queen on the e-file and allows the
decisive 131 Kh4 Qh6+ 132 Nh5 etc.  That is the losing continuation
played in the game.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129.e5 Qa2+ 130.Kh3 is the famous
130… move of the 136-move Game 6. White’s king is on h3, Ng3, Rf5, e5 and
the black king is on e8. White’s two winning ideas are e6–e7–e8 and
Rxe5 with the rook landing on e5.  

The e6 push is covered by the a2–e6 diagonal and the e5 square is
covered by the a1–e5 diagonal.  Keeping the queen on a file, or on the
2nd rank where it can be shuffled back to the h-file for Qh2+ / Qg2+
perpetuals, keeps the e-pawn under control and takes the queen out of
the Rf5–e5 net.  

The classic textbook illustration is the a-file retreat

130…Qa1 !

which puts the queen on a1–e5 and allows the perpetual a1–h1+,
h1–a1… It is the same idea on the a-file with any waiting retreat
Qa3, Qa4, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8, and on the 2nd rank with the waiting moves
Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2.  The move most often quoted in the literature is
the one-move waiting move

130…Qa3

which is equivalent to Qa1 in practice.  Qg2+, Qh2+ and the e-file
moves Qe6, Qe2 and the 5th-rank move Qa5 lose the queen to Rxe5 or to
Kxg2 / Kxh2, so they are the losing moves.  The e-file / 5th-rank
moves Qe2 and Qa5 in particular allow 131.Rxe5 with a winning
recapture for White.  That is the blunder actually played, 130…Qe6,
and the whole family of a-file / 2nd-rank waits is the drawing
resource that Nepo missed.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129…Qa2+ 130.Kh3 is Black queen on a2, White King h3, Knight g3, Rook f5, pawn e5, Black King e8. White’s two threats are Rxe5 and e6/e7-e8. The queen has to keep the e5-pawn under attack if Rxe5 is to be met, and it has to be able to give a perpetual on the king on h3. 

Reachable squares from a2 that attack e5 are b2, e2, h2 and a1 and a5. Reachable squares that attack e6 are e2, a6 and the diagonal b3/c4/d5. The only one-reach square that attacks both e5 and e6 is e2. In practice the draw is obtained by a waiting move which keeps the queen in perpetual-checking distance of h3 and which keeps the e5-pawn covered, so that any e6 is met with checks and any Rxe5 is met by Qxe5.

The literature that is quoted in the deliberation points to the a-file waiting moves and the 2nd-rank waiting moves as the drawing family. Colleague 1,2,5 all stress the a-file retreats Qa1/Qa3 and the 2nd-rank family Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2/Qf2 as the standard perpetual resources. Qa1 is the text-book illustration, Qa3 is the most forcing a-file waiting move, and the 2nd-rank moves keep the queen on the 2nd rank for the Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetual. 

Qg2+ and Qh2+ are immediate checks which lose the queen, Qe6 is the actual losing blunder because it allows Rxe5 with the queen on the e-file, and Qa5 on the 5th rank is vulnerable to Rxe5. The consensus in the room is that the draw is obtained with a1/a3 on the a-file and with b2/e2 on the 2nd rank. The moves most often singled out are A Qa1 and N Qa3, with E Qb2 and M Qe2 also satisfying the e5-cover/perpetual idea. B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4, J Qa5 are a-file squares that are normally quoted as the same idea, though Qa5 is the one most frequently flagged as suffering from the Rxe5 refutation in Colleague 3’s analysis. The disagreement is on the exact size of the drawing set – a-file only vs a-file + 2nd-rank – but Qa1/Qa3/Qb2/Qe2 are the moves repeatedly identified as drawing.

Reachable squares from a2 that attack e5 are b2, e2, h2 and a1 and a5. Reachable squares that attack e6 are e2, a6 and the diagonal b3/c4/d5. However, the 2nd-rank options (Qb2–Qf2) carry a subtle risk once White plays Rf3 or maneuvers the knight to f5/f7; the queen can be harassed by the rook without an immediate safe square on the same rank. By contrast, the a-file retreats keep the queen farther from the rook–knight coordination and still threaten the Ng3 blocker directly.
